reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Multisystem disorder characterised by benign hamartomas affecting the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and eyes
Skin findings include hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf spots), facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, and periungual fibromas

Neurological features include cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, epilepsy (often including infantile spasms), and cognitive and behavioural difficulties within the TSC-associated neuropsychiatric spectrum
Cardiac rhabdomyomas may be detected antenatally or in infancy and often regress spontaneously
Renal angiomyolipomas and cysts can bleed or impair function and require surveillance
Caused by mutations in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), tumour suppressors that normally restrain the mTOR signalling pathway
Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity and a high rate of de novo mutations
mTOR inhibitor therapy can shrink certain lesions such as subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and angiomyolipomas under specialist care
reference.pathophysiology: Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1, encoding hamartin, or TSC2, encoding tuberin. Together these proteins form a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway, which controls cell growth and proliferation. Loss of function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive mTOR activation and the growth of benign hamartomatous lesions across multiple organs. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, though many cases are de novo, and lesion formation is consistent with a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining allele. The mechanistic understanding underpins the therapeutic use of mTOR inhibitors.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated epilepsy or infantile spasms of other cause
Multiple endocrine neoplasia and other hamartoma syndromes
Vitiligo or other causes of hypopigmented macules
additionalInvestigations: Assessment against established clinical diagnostic criteria supported by TSC1 or TSC2 molecular testing
Brain magnetic resonance imaging for tubers, subependymal nodules, and giant cell astrocytomas
Renal imaging for angiomyolipomas and cysts
Echocardiography, ophthalmological examination, and skin assessment, with neurodevelopmental evaluation
redFlags: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma causing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure requiring urgent intervention
Poorly controlled seizures, including infantile spasms, which need prompt treatment to protect development
Large or bleeding renal angiomyolipomas with risk of life-threatening haemorrhage
Cardiac rhabdomyomas causing outflow obstruction or arrhythmia in infancy
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable; many individuals live full lives, but epilepsy severity, cognitive impairment, and organ complications such as giant cell astrocytomas and renal or pulmonary disease determine morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Overlooking subtle skin signs such as hypomelanotic macules that aid early diagnosis
Failing to arrange surveillance for growing subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and renal lesions
Delaying treatment of infantile spasms with consequences for development
Not recognising the neuropsychiatric spectrum and its impact on quality of life
management: Use mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and growing renal angiomyolipomas, and topical sirolimus for facial angiofibromas
Manage epilepsy with antiseizure medication, using vigabatrin as first-line for infantile spasms, and consider epilepsy surgery or vagus nerve stimulation in refractory cases
Treat renal angiomyolipomas at risk of haemorrhage with an mTOR inhibitor or selective arterial embolisation, preserving nephrons
Undertake regular surveillance with brain MRI, renal imaging, echocardiography, and ophthalmological and skin review
Assess and support the TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders including learning, behavioural and cognitive difficulties
Coordinate multidisciplinary care and offer genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 mutation
